userStories.title: iOS ships English-only while Android ships Spanish, and the localization guard reads as though a migration is under way
userStories.description: As a Spanish-speaking seller, I want the iOS app in my language, or I want the team to have decided on purpose that it will not be - because today Android speaks Spanish, iOS does not, and no one chose that.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE FIRST whether iOS is meant to be localized at all. Android has values-es/ and its CI fails on MissingTranslation, so the two clients already disagree about whether a non-English seller is a customer. That is a product call, not a cleanup

If iOS IS meant to be localized: Localizable.xcstrings currently has ZERO entries, so decide whether the catalog is committed (translations live in git and can be reviewed) or generated at build time (translations live nowhere). Today it is the second, which is why nothing is translated

If iOS is NOT meant to be localized: say so in ios/Scripts/no-bare-strings.py, because its docstring describes a migration that is widening and that sentence is what makes the BASELINE read as temporary
Either way the guard must stop being a step that only fails AFTER the simulator build. It caught US-1866 five days late because it runs at ios-ci.yml:128, behind the slowest job in the lane
Reconcile the scope: SCOPE_DIRS covers Prospect/Vision/Speech/Settings and the docstring says the other ~670 app-wide strings are deliberately unscoped. Confirm that is still the intent
userStories.notes: [P3][iOS/Localization] Filed 2026-08-12 while fixing a red iOS CI lane. THE MEASUREMENT THAT PROMPTED IT: ios/GradeThread/Localizable.xcstrings parses as valid JSON with sourceLanguage en and strings: {} - zero entries. So not one iOS string has ever been translated, including every string in the US-1224 and US-1155 BASELINE sets that the guard describes as migrated. SWIFT_EMIT_LOC_STRINGS=YES populates the catalog at build time on the Mac and the result is not committed, so the artifact the guard validates is permanently empty by construction. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GUARD, which is why this is worth a story rather than a shrug: no-bare-strings.py tells you to localize via a string key OR update BASELINE, and in this repo those are the same action - a SwiftUI Text("...") IS a LocalizedStringKey, so a bare literal is already as localized as anything gets here. What the guard actually buys is a human acknowledging new UI copy, which is worth having, but the docstring sells it as a migration checkpoint and that framing is what makes each BASELINE addition feel like debt rather than a decision. THE CROSS-PLATFORM HALF: Android does the opposite. values-es/strings.xml is real, lintDebug treats MissingTranslation as an ERROR, and US-2492 (Sourcing Radar on Android, in flight as this was filed) is required to ship Spanish for the SAME feature whose iOS strings are English-only. Two clients, one product, opposite answers about whether a Spanish-speaking seller is a customer - and nobody chose that. | 2026-08-12 AC4 DONE. The localization guard now runs as the fourth of four Python lints, ahead of brew, xcodegen and the simulator build. It needed no toolchain and no generated project, so there was never a reason for it to wait behind them - and waiting is why US-1866 failure surfaced at the slowest point in the lane and sat red on main for five days. Verified by parsing the YAML and asserting the step index is before both xcodegen and the build, plus exactly one run line so the step MOVED rather than duplicated. REMAINING: AC1 is the product call (is iOS meant to be localized at all), AC2 follows from it (commit the catalog or accept that it is generated and empty), AC3 is the docstring rewrite that depends on AC1, and AC5 is the SCOPE_DIRS confirmation.

userStories.title: iOS sells buyer tools in every plan and ships no way to use them
userStories.description: As a FlipDesk subscriber on iPhone, I want the buyer tools my plan includes, so that I get what the pricing page sold me.
acceptanceCriteria: src/lib/constants.ts SELLER_PLAN_BUYER_TIER bundles Guard into Starter/Pro and Connoisseur into Business, and /pricing states 'Every FlipDesk plan includes buyer tools'. A grep of ios/**/*.swift for conditionAlert, fitPrediction, portfolio, trustScore, purchaseGuarantee and demandBoard currently returns zero matches.

Ship iOS screens for the app-deliverable bundled capabilities: condition alerts, closet portfolio, buyer trust score and purchase-guarantee coverage. The browser-extension second opinion is out of scope (desktop-only by nature) and must be stated as such on the iOS plan screen.
Each new iOS screen reads its gate from the same buyer entitlement payload the web useBuyerEntitlements hook consumes, so a plan change is reflected on both clients without a second source of truth.
An iOS UI or unit test asserts that a Business-tier entitlement payload unlocks the Connoisseur-gated screens and a free payload locks them.
The iOS plan screen lists exactly the bundled buyer capabilities that iOS can actually deliver — no bullet advertises a screen that does not exist.
userStories.notes: SLICE 1 of N SHIPPED - the story is NOT done and is deliberately left open.  The deferral note said what these two need: a macOS session, or decomposition into slices small enough that a CI round-trip per slice is an acceptable feedback loop, entitlement plumbing first. This is that first slice, and it is fully verifiable from Windows.  SHIPPED: GET /api/buyer/entitlements, serving the resolved {plan, gateFlags, allowances} payload from the existing edge resolver (lib/buyer-entitlements.ts) that every buyer route already gates on via requireBuyerFeature. No new logic - it exposes an answer that was already being computed.  WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT FIRST SLICE. AC3 requires iOS to read its gate from the same payload the web hook consumes, without a second source of truth. But the web hook resolves the matrix CLIENT-SIDE from the profile it already holds - there was no endpoint to read. A Swift reimplementation of the matrix would have been exactly the second source of truth AC3 forbids, and the kind that lets a plan change unlock a feature on one client and not the other. So the server resolves it once and both clients read it. Without this, AC3 was not satisfiable by any amount of Swift.  Fail-safe direction is deliberate: a users-row read failure returns the FREE payload (new FREE_BUYER_ENTITLEMENTS) with 200 rather than 500. A locked screen with a retry is a better outcome than an error page, and it can never over-grant - an over-grant shows a paid screen to someone who is not paying. no-store, private on both paths so a plan change shows on the next load and no shared cache can hand one buyer's entitlements to another.  US-268: the route takes no id, filter or workspace header; getBuyerEntitlements reads c.get(userId)'s own row. Two tenant-isolation_test.ts cases added (requires auth; answers for the caller and exposes only the resolved payload, with a supplied ?user_id ignored). Edge suite green: 17 passed, 177 ignored.  STILL OPEN, and blocked on a macOS toolchain, NOT on design: AC2 the four iOS screens (condition alerts, closet portfolio, buyer trust score, purchase-guarantee coverage); AC4 the iOS test asserting a Business payload unlocks Connoisseur-gated screens and a free payload locks them; AC5 the iOS plan screen listing exactly the deliverable bundled capabilities, with the browser-extension second opinion stated as desktop-only. Each of those is Swift that cannot be compiled, run or tested from this Windows checkout, and writing it unverified would ship code whose first compile is in CI.  AC1's premise re-verified today: a grep of ios for conditionAlert, fitPrediction, portfolio, trustScore, purchaseGuarantee and demandBoard still returns zero matches.  Guard: src/test/buyer-entitlements-contract.test.ts, 10 cases, 6 proven red. It deliberately asserts NOTHING about iOS screens existing - a guard that goes green while the feature does not exist is the failure mode it is written to prevent. When the screens land, that file is what they extend. | SLICE 2 SHIPPED 2026-08-14, story STILL OPEN. AC2's four screens, AC4's iOS test and AC5's Swift plan screen all need macOS. This is the part of AC5 that does not.  AC5 says the iOS plan screen lists exactly what iOS can deliver and no bullet advertises a screen that does not exist. That is a property, and nothing held it - the classification of which of the 13 bundled buyer capabilities iOS can actually deliver existed only in this story's prose. So the Swift author would have written the bullet list by reading the story and deciding, which is the same act that produced the over-promise in the first place.  Extended the EXISTING registry rather than adding a parallel one. src/lib/buyer-features.ts already keys every capability by BuyerGateFlags with a live flag meaning does the WEB surface exist - which was the only question worth asking while there was one client. Added ios: shipped | planned | desktop-only alongside it. Because the record is Record<keyof BuyerGateFlags, ...>, a NEW buyer capability now does not compile until somebody classifies it. The default is decide, never quietly becomes an iOS bullet, which is the failure this whole story is an instance of.  Only ONE capability is desktop-only for a reason about the capability rather than about effort: the extension second opinion IS a browser extension that reads the marketplace page you are looking at. Four more ride inside that check (discrepancy scoring, price fairness, fit prediction) or are bought against a grade on the web (authenticity add-on). Each carries the sentence the plan screen will show, because AC2 says the extension must be STATED as desktop-only rather than quietly omitted - a bundled capability that just vanishes on one client reads as a bug, and a subscriber who paid for the bundle is owed the explanation.  THE GUARD WAS WRONG ON FIRST WRITE, in the one direction that mattered, and this is the part worth keeping. Its check for advertising a screen that does not exist was a COUNT: at most two capabilities may claim shipped. I broke it on purpose by flipping trustScore from planned to shipped, and it stayed GREEN, because the count was still under the limit. The single thing the guard existed to catch was the thing it let through. A threshold is not a property.  Replaced with an iosScreen field required when ios is shipped, naming the Swift file, and the guard asserts that file EXISTS on disk. Now the same break fails and names the offender. AC5 read literally - no bullet advertises a screen that does not exist - is checkable rather than an honour system.  Also removed a vacuous assertion I had written into the same file: ["ios/GradeThread"].flatMap(() => []) compared to [] is always true. Caught before it shipped, but it is the fourth vacuous check this loop and they all look like tests.  STILL OPEN and blocked on macOS, unchanged: AC2's four screens (condition alerts, closet portfolio, buyer trust score, purchase-guarantee coverage), AC4's entitlement test, AC5's Swift screen itself. Slice 1 (74a2be2a) already serves the entitlement payload those screens gate on.  Guard: src/test/buyer-ios-delivery.test.ts, 9 cases, verified to bite twice (once finding its own weakness). Verified: tsc -b, lint 16 warnings 0 errors baseline, ui:check 0, 4095 web tests, vault:lint green, runbook-sync green. No migration.

userStories.title: Walk-around video grading is web-only, on the platform without the camera
userStories.description: As a seller grading on my phone, I want to record one walk-around clip instead of staging four photos, so that I can grade an item in one pass.
acceptanceCriteria: src/pages/new-submission.tsx:217 offers captureMode 'photos' | 'video' and POSTs video plus video_grading=true to /api/grade/submit. A grep of ios/**/*.swift for AVCaptureMovie, videoURL, walkaround or video_grading returns zero matches.
iOS capture offers a walk-around video mode that posts the same multipart fields the web path sends (video, video_grading, video_slot_marks, video_capture_source).
A clip that yields no usable required view lands the submission in needs_photos and is not charged, matching the web behaviour at new-submission.tsx:877-892.
Upload progress is shown for the clip; a 60 MB upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a hang.
userStories.notes: SLICE 1 of N SHIPPED - the story is NOT done and is deliberately left open.  AC3's PREMISE IS UNDERSOLD, and that is the most useful thing found here. It describes the no-charge behaviour as matching the web behaviour at new-submission.tsx:877-892, but the guarantee is the SERVER's, not the page's: failVideoGrading in routes/grade.ts returns BEFORE payment precedence runs, refunds a buyer meter debit taken at the gate, sets needs_photos with video_graded false, and answers payment paid:false charged:false. Any client posting the contract inherits that. So AC3 needs NO iOS work at all - and iOS must not implement a client-side do-not-charge, because that is not a guarantee.  SHIPPED: src/lib/video-grading-contract.ts pins the multipart field names (video, video_grading, video_slot_marks, video_capture_source), the exact opt-in string, the two capture sources, and the abstain response shape with an isVideoAbstain helper. new-submission.tsx now APPENDS from those constants instead of spelling the strings inline.  WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT FIRST SLICE. AC2 asks iOS to post the same multipart fields the web path sends. Those names were a private handshake between two files - spelled in new-submission.tsx, read in routes/grade.ts - which is fine with one client and a trap with two: a native client would have to reverse-engineer them out of page code, and a rename on either side would silently break whichever client nobody was looking at. Now there is a spec to implement.  The opt-in is worth calling out: the server compares against the literal string true, so a native client sending 1, TRUE or a JSON boolean would ATTACH a clip and then be graded from photos it never sent. The contract records that and the guard asserts the server still compares exactly.  STILL OPEN, blocked on a macOS toolchain: AC2's actual recorder (AVCapture walk-around mode) and AC4's upload progress - a 60MB upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a hang. Both are Swift that cannot be compiled or run from this Windows checkout.  AC1's premise re-verified: a grep of ios for AVCaptureMovie, videoURL, walkaround and video_grading still returns zero matches.  Guard: src/test/video-grading-contract.test.ts, 11 cases, but only 1 proven red - and that is honest, not weak. Most of these assertions PIN behaviour that already existed (the edge field reads, the abstain path, the refund) so a second client can rely on it and a refactor cannot quietly move the charge earlier. Only the web-side wiring to the constants is new. The file asserts NOTHING about an iOS recorder existing. | SLICE 2 SHIPPED 2026-08-14, story STILL OPEN. AC2's recorder and AC4's progress UI are Swift and need macOS.  AC4's WEB half turns out to be already done and correct - new-submission.tsx routes the video POST through XMLHttpRequest precisely because fetch has no upload-progress event, with the 60 MB reads-as-a-hang reasoning already in the comment. So nothing to fix there. What slice 1 had NOT recorded is the set of rules a recorder has to be BUILT to, and getting those wrong produces clips the server refuses after the entire upload has gone up a phone connection.  THE SHARPEST FIND: THE LIMITS THAT APPLY ARE THE ROUTE'S, AND THEY ARE NOT THE VALIDATION LIBRARY'S. lib/video-validation.ts defaults to 100 MB and 60 seconds. routes/grade.ts passes its own MAX_VIDEO_BYTES of 60 MB and MAX_VIDEO_DURATION_SECONDS of 45. A Swift author reading the validator - the obvious place to look for what a video upload may be - would build a recorder producing 100 MB, 60-second clips that are rejected every time. Both numbers are now in the contract and the guard reads them back out of the ROUTE, and also asserts the library's really are looser, since that gap is the trap.  SECOND: PHOTOS AND A CLIP ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, and this is the rule a second client is most likely to break, because the natural iOS flow is additive - stage photos, then also record a walk-around, which feels like sending more evidence. videoPhotoConflict refuses it with a 400. Two reasons worth keeping: the pipeline makes one Vision call per image, so accepting both stacks the 14-slot photo cap on top of the frame cap for one grade's revenue with nothing bounding the request; and it voids the claim the feature is sold on, that every graded view came from one continuous take. So the client must make it a MODE, not an addition.  THIRD, for AC4 one step later: 100 percent uploaded is not 100 percent done. Frame extraction and grading run after the last byte and the server sends no progress for that phase. The web holds the bar at 100 and lets the copy carry the rest. A client that dismisses the sheet at 100 tells the seller their grade is ready while the server has not started.  Also added videoSubmitRejection so a client can refuse a clip BEFORE spending the upload, mirroring the server's order - the photo conflict is reported first, because it is the one thing the seller can fix without re-recording. An UNREADABLE duration deliberately passes through to the server rather than being guessed at locally: null means the client could not read it, which is not the same as knowing it is bad, and guessing would block clips the server would have taken.  A VERIFICATION FLAW FOUND AND FIXED, and it affected this whole loop. I had been running npx tsc -b piped to tail followed by echo TSC-OK. A shell pipeline reports the exit status of the LAST command, so that printed TSC-OK unconditionally - and this iteration it printed TSC-OK directly underneath a real TS2532. Earlier runs were genuinely clean (they printed no errors above the marker) but the check was unsound throughout. Now running the command bare and reading its exit code.  STILL OPEN, blocked on macOS: AC2's AVCapture walk-around recorder and AC4's iOS progress UI. Guard: src/test/video-grading-contract.test.ts, now 25 cases (14 new), verified to bite - drifted the caps to the library defaults and dropped the photo conflict, 3 cases went red naming each. Verified: tsc -b exit 0, lint exit 0, ui:check exit 0, 4109 web tests, deno check exit 0, vault:lint green. No migration.

userStories.title: The Terms of Service predate four shipped products
userStories.description: As the business, I want the Terms to cover what we actually sell, so that our terms match our product.
acceptanceCriteria: src/pages/legal/terms.tsx is effective April 1, 2026 and contains zero occurrences of 'buyer plan', 'in-app purchase', 'App Store', 'Google Play', 'extension' or 'consignment'.

Terms cover: buyer subscriptions as a second paid product with its own cancellation; store-billed subscriptions where Apple and Google own refunds and cancellation; the Lister browser extension automating the user's own logged-in marketplace sessions; and consignment, which involves holding third-party goods and paying consignors via Stripe Connect.
The extension section is consistent with the in-product risk disclosure already written at src/pages/flipdesk/marketplaces.tsx:1495-1532.
The AUP is reviewed in the same pass; it carries the same April 1, 2026 date.
This story is legal review, not engineering — it ships when counsel signs off on the copy.
userStories.notes: BLOCKED ON COUNSEL, not on engineering — AC5 says so explicitly ('it ships when counsel signs off on the copy'), so this stays OPEN. What I did do (2026-08-14, commit below): verified all four gaps against the CODE rather than assuming them, and wrote docs/legal/terms-update-brief-2026-08.md — a brief for counsel with, per gap, what shipped, what the current Terms say, why the two conflict, and DRAFT language marked as draft. Nothing is wired to the live page; terms.tsx is untouched and its April 1 date still stands. The four confirmed gaps: (1) the buyer subscription is a SECOND independent paid product while section 3 describes one subscription in the singular, so a buyer who cancels from the seller Billing page has not cancelled what they think they cancelled; (2) store-billed subscriptions — section 3 says billed through Stripe and cancel in-app, and for an IAP subscriber BOTH sentences are false, with refunds being Apple's or Google's decision rather than ours to grant or refuse; (3) the Lister extension automates the seller's OWN logged-in session on five platforms whose terms restrict automation, which section 8's generic third-party clause does not describe — the draft reuses the four facts the product ALREADY discloses in src/lib/marketplace-disclosure.ts, and I flagged that the AUP's blanket 'scraping' prohibition can be read against our own extension; (4) consignment now involves goods the customer does not own and payouts through Stripe Connect to someone who is not our customer, and the Terms say nothing at all — that clause is the one most in need of a lawyer, so the draft is deliberately narrow. The AUP carries the same April 1 date and is listed for the same pass. Noted for the follow-up commit: a guard test asserting the Terms' extension section carries the same four facts as the in-product disclosure, so the two cannot drift. | FOLLOW-UP SHIPPED, story still OPEN - AC5 blocks it on counsel and nothing here writes legal copy. terms.tsx and acceptable-use.tsx are untouched.  SHIPPED: src/test/legal-extension-disclosure-parity.test.ts, the drift guard the previous note promised. It is written to be honest in BOTH states. While the Terms carry no extension section it asserts that absence is still tracked as open work, so it cannot pass vacuously; the moment a section lands it starts checking that all four disclosed facts are present, matching on the CLAIM rather than the wording so counsel can rephrase freely. It also fails if the Terms and AUP effective dates diverge, which is AC4, and it pins that the four mechanism facts are single-sourced in marketplace-disclosure.ts and come FIRST - a per-platform note (Poshmark's share caps, Grailed's manual delist) is appended and can never displace one of the four.  CORRECTED A FLAG I RAISED IN THE PREVIOUS NOTE. I had written that the AUP's blanket scraping prohibition could be read against our own Lister extension and was worth a carve-out. Re-reading the clause, that is wrong: BOTH the automated-access and the scraping clauses are scoped to the Service - GradeThread - while the extension automates the seller's own signed-in eBay/Poshmark/Mercari session and reads MARKETPLACE pages, and where it does talk to GradeThread it uses our documented API. So there is no self-contradiction and no carve-out is needed. The brief now carries the correction with the reasoning visible rather than the flag deleted, so counsel is not billed for resolving a conflict that does not exist. The guard asserts the scoping, so if either clause is ever broadened past the Service the question comes back on its own.  STILL OPEN and genuinely blocked: the four Terms sections themselves (buyer subscriptions as a second paid product with its own cancellation; store-billed subscriptions where Apple and Google own refunds; the Lister extension; consignment goods and Stripe Connect payouts) plus the AUP pass. Draft language for each is in docs/legal/terms-update-brief-2026-08.md, marked as draft and deliberately not wired to the live page - the guard fails if any of it reaches terms.tsx without sign-off.  Guard: 10 cases, all green on the current tree BY DESIGN. This one pins existing behaviour and arms a future check rather than fixing a defect; the red-before-green shape does not apply and claiming otherwise would be a false report.

userStories.title: Shopify can be connected on web but not on iOS
userStories.description: As a subscriber paying the same price on iPhone, I want to connect my Shopify store, so that my plan works the same on both clients.
acceptanceCriteria: ios/GradeThread/Marketplaces/MarketplacesView.swift:176 states 'Shopify is web-only, and is the sole .api entry in phasedChannels'. The web page renders ShopifySetup at src/pages/flipdesk/marketplaces.tsx:1413.
iOS offers the Shopify connection flow, or the iOS Marketplaces screen states plainly that Shopify is connected on the web and links there.
Whichever is chosen, the iOS plan and marketplace screens never imply a capability the client cannot deliver.
userStories.notes: DEFERRED 2026-08-14 — iOS-only, and this checkout cannot verify Swift. Windows has no swiftc or xcodebuild, and the macOS 'iOS CI' lane only runs on a PUSH, which the standing rule forbids for this branch (it holds migrations 00592 and 00593 awaiting the owner's prod apply). So Swift written here would sit unbuilt and untested in a local commit for an unknown length of time, and the first thing anyone would learn about a syntax error is a red lane after the migrations finally land. That is a worse position than the gap itself. Same reasoning already recorded on US-2503 and US-2504. What is NOT blocked and has been done for the web/edge halves this loop touched: US-2525's edge attachment endpoints are client-agnostic, so the iOS half is a UI story (US-2561) rather than a protocol one. Pick these up in a macOS session, or after the held migrations are applied and the branch can push to CI. | SLICE SHIPPED, story still OPEN - and the premise turned out to be mostly STALE, which is the finding worth recording.  Reading the Swift (this checkout can READ it; what it cannot do is compile it), AC2's second branch is already substantially satisfied and AC3 is satisfied outright. MarketplacesView.swift badges Shopify 'Live - manage on web', its ChannelTier comment says Shopify is web-only and eBay is the in-app one, and the help text says in prose that Shopify connects via API on the web dashboard. The iOS paywall never mentions Shopify or marketplaces at all. So the iOS client does NOT advertise a capability it cannot deliver - the thing AC3 exists to prevent.  The real remaining gap is narrower than the title suggests: AC2 says the screen should say Shopify is web-managed AND LINK THERE. It says it; it does not link. That link is a Swift edit and stays blocked.  SHIPPED: src/test/ios-marketplace-capability-parity.test.ts, following the existing ios-*-parity guards that scan Swift as TEXT from the web suite so a Windows checkout can still enforce a cross-client contract. It asserts the badge still names the web, that no in-app Shopify connect affordance appears (connectShopify / shopifyOAuth / startShopify), that Shopify is still PRESENT in the channel list - dropping it would satisfy 'never implies a capability' by hiding a product the seller pays for, which is not the fix - and that the Swift's claim to mirror web MARKETPLACE_TIER is true, so a web-side mechanism change cannot leave the iOS badge describing something that no longer exists. It also asserts the paywall names no marketplace.  The guard was verified to BITE, not just to pass: shortening the badge to 'Live' turns two cases red. All-green on the current tree is the correct result here because this pins existing honesty rather than fixing a defect, and claiming a red-before-green would be a false report.  STILL OPEN: the 'and links there' half of AC2, or AC2's first branch (ship the in-app connection flow). Both are Swift. | 2026-08-15 THE HELD-MIGRATION WORDING ABOVE IS HISTORICAL, RESOLVED. The owner applied every outstanding migration and pushed main; origin/main and local are the same commit, PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md lists no HELD section, and the session-context hook reports none. So nothing in this story is waiting on a prod apply and the branch is not frozen on its account. Recorded as an appended correction rather than by editing the sentence, because these notes are append-only and prd-lint resolves by segment order. WHY THIS GETS ITS OWN NOTE INSTEAD OF BEING LEFT TO ROT: HELD is not a status, it is an instruction to stop, and a stale one tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not. That has cost real sessions in this repo (US-2286's 2026-08-09 note says so explicitly). VERIFY IT RATHER THAN TRUST THIS: curl -fsS https://functions.gradethread.com/health/ready | jq .schema — US-2603 added a missing[] listing versions this build ships that the database never recorded, which is the check a bare status:match cannot do. | 2026-08-15 STATUS CORRECTION, formal: no migration named in this story is held. Every outstanding migration is applied to prod and main is pushed (origin/main == local). The previous segment said this in words prd-lint does not recognise, so the guard kept warning; this one uses the token it reads.

userStories.title: The two onboardings ask different questions and iOS throws the answer away
userStories.description: As a user who answered the onboarding question once, I want both clients to remember it, so that I am not shown a generic dashboard forever.
acceptanceCriteria: Web writes users.use_case as seller | buyer | consignment | developer and personalizes quick actions, feature cards and the first-run CTA from it (src/pages/dashboard.tsx:126-261). iOS asks reseller | grader | store (ios/GradeThread/Onboarding/OnboardingState.swift:14-20) and sends the answer only to telemetry (OnboardingView.swift:183).
The two clients share one use-case taxonomy.
iOS persists the choice to the same users.use_case column the web dashboard reads.
A user who onboards on iOS and then opens the web dashboard sees the persona-tailored version, not the default branch.
userStories.notes: DEFERRED 2026-08-14 — the deliverable is on iOS, which this checkout cannot verify (no swiftc/xcodebuild on Windows; the macOS lane only runs on a push this branch must not make while 00592/00593 are held). But the blocker underneath it is a PRODUCT DECISION, not a build one, and it needs the owner's answer before anyone writes code on either side. The two taxonomies do not map cleanly. Web writes users.use_case with a DB CHECK constraint (migration 00022) allowing exactly: seller, buyer, consignment, developer. iOS asks three questions that describe VOLUME and CHANNEL rather than persona: reseller ('I resell at volume'), grader ('I grade & sell a few'), store ('I run an eBay store'). Both of the first two are 'seller' on the web taxonomy, so mapping them loses the only distinction iOS was collecting; 'store' is arguably seller OR consignment. Three ways forward, and they are not equivalent: (A) map iOS onto the existing four and accept that reseller and grader collapse into one — cheapest, no migration, and the web dashboard immediately personalizes for an iOS user; (B) widen the CHECK constraint to carry volume as a second dimension — a migration, and the web dashboard's branching (dashboard.tsx:126-261) would need to decide what to do with the new values; (C) keep them separate and have iOS send its answer to a NEW column, which is the status quo dressed up. I recommend (A) with reseller and store both mapping to 'seller' and grader to 'seller' as well, treating volume as telemetry rather than persona — because the four web values answer 'what is this person here to do' and all three iOS answers are 'sell', which is exactly why the collapse is honest rather than lossy. But that is the owner's call, not mine to ship. No code written. | PRODUCT DECISION MADE by the owner 2026-08-14: option A - map all three iOS answers to seller, keep reseller/grader/store as telemetry only. The three options and the recommendation had been sitting in this note unanswered for several iterations; I put them in front of the owner as a direct question instead, which is what unblocked it. Lesson: a decision buried in a prd note is not a decision requested.  SLICE SHIPPED, story still OPEN. New src/lib/use-case-taxonomy.ts pins the decision as the SPEC the Swift side implements: the four canonical values (mirroring the 00022 CHECK exactly), the three iOS answers, the mapping, and an isWritableUseCase guard so nothing the map produces can be rejected by Postgres at runtime on the phone after onboarding has already reported success. And AC4 needs no dashboard change: dashboard.tsx already collapses case seller into default, so an iOS user goes from NULL to seller on the SAME branch. The difference is not cosmetic though, which is why persisting still matters: activation-checklist.tsx branches on useCase === seller explicitly and a NULL user misses it.  The guard reads the OnboardingUseCase enum BODY out of the Swift and compares the WHOLE set, so a fourth iOS answer is a red test rather than an answer that silently writes nothing. userStories.title: iOS shows no unread notification count on the tab bar
userStories.description: As a seller or buyer using the iPhone app, I want an unread count on the tab bar, so that I learn about a new offer or return without opening the app and hunting.
acceptanceCriteria: No badge API is used anywhere in ios/GradeThread — a grep for applicationIconBadge, badgeCount and .badge( over the Swift tree finds only unrelated matches in InventoryFilterSheet and ToolsHubView.

The unread source already exists and needs no new backend: public.notifications (migration 00007) with is_read, RLS-scoped to auth.uid(). Web reads it directly through the authenticated Supabase client in src/components/dashboard/notification-center.tsx; iOS can do the same.
The count badges the relevant tab in ContentView.swift's TabView and clears as rows are marked read, matching the web centre's behaviour.
Set the app icon badge from the same count so it is visible with the app closed, since the transactional-push path (lib/transactional-push.ts) already delivers these events to APNs.

AC3 and AC4's Swift halves need macOS; the iOS CI lane on macOS runners is the gate and nothing here was built or run against a simulator.  AC1 premise VERIFIED exactly as filed: grepping the Swift tree for applicationIconBadge, badgeCount and .badge( finds only InventoryFilterSheet and ToolsHubView, both unrelated. AC2 verified too - notification-center.tsx reads public.notifications through the authenticated client, so iOS needs no new backend.  But two things the Swift half READS FROM were wrong, and both would have made the iOS work look broken while being correct.  1. NO PUSH HAS EVER CARRIED A BADGE. PushPayload.badge has existed in apns.ts since pushes shipped and buildBody copies it into the aps dictionary - and no caller anywhere has ever set it. So the app-icon number AC4 asks for could not appear no matter what Swift did, because the only thing that can badge a CLOSED app is the payload. New lib/notification-badge.ts counts unread rows and safePush attaches it.  The seam is deliberate in both directions. Not per-helper, because there are a dozen and the next one forgets. Not in sendPushToUser, because that is the transport and it also serves pushes with no notification behind them (cross-listing progress), which would get a number about something else. safePush is the one place every transactional push passes and nothing else does.  THE SHARP EDGE, and the reason this is a named helper rather than one line: in APNs an ABSENT badge key means leave the icon alone and a badge of 0 means CLEAR it. Opposite behaviours, one missing key. So no badge is attached when the count cannot be read (a database hiccup must not wipe a badge showing five unread) or when it is genuinely 0 (pushTokenExpiring and pushSaleCreated have no notification row, and must not clear a badge they know nothing about). The consequence, stated rather than discovered later: the server only ever RAISES the badge. Clearing it is the app's job on the same signal that marks rows read.  2. THE WEB BELL COUNTED A PAGE, NOT THE ROWS. unreadCount was notifications.filter(not is_read).length over a limit-20 fetch, so it stopped counting at 20 - and its own 99+ render branch was unreachable. AC3 says the iOS badge should match the web centre, so matching it would have shipped the cap to the phone, and AC4's server count would have disagreed with the bell on the same account with neither number obviously wrong. Now a head+exact count query, paired with the list on every refresh path.  That fix exposed a THIRD bug underneath it. Mark all read collected ids from the same 20-row page and marked those, so on an account with more unread than that it left the rest unread - invisible while the badge came from the same page (it read 20, you clicked, it read 0) and glaring once the count is real. Now an update by predicate. Chained .eq, never .or: US-1552, prod PostgREST rejects logical operators on a mutation and the local stack accepts them, so CI cannot catch it. The break script's replace silently no-op'd because the file is CRLF and my search string was LF, and one assertion only checked that withUnreadBadge appeared in the file, which the IMPORT line satisfies on its own. An import is not a use. Both fixed, then re-verified red. userStories.description: As an iOS user reporting a problem with a photo, I want to attach the photo and close my own ticket, so that the app is not the one client where support is text only.
acceptanceCriteria: US-2525 shipped attachments and a user-side close on web + edge. ios/GradeThread/Support/SupportTicketsView.swift sends body text only and offers no close.

The composer and the reply box each accept up to 3 images (MAX_ATTACHMENTS_PER_MESSAGE), sent as data URLs on the existing POST /api/support-tickets and POST /api/support-tickets/:id/messages — no new endpoint.
A thread message renders its attachments from the signed urls the GET returns, and shows a placeholder rather than a broken image when a url has expired (TTL is 600s).
A Close button calls POST /api/support-tickets/:id/close and the row reflects the closed status; replying reopens it, matching web.

ALL FIVE AC PREMISES VERIFIED against the running code rather than assumed. AC2's endpoints all exist and need no additions: POST /api/support-tickets, POST /:id/messages, POST /:id/close, GET /:id. MAX_ATTACHMENTS_PER_MESSAGE is 3. ATTACHMENT_URL_TTL_SEC is 600, under the 900s US-276 caps the private bucket at. The validator allows jpeg, png, webp. The reopen rule is the server's, not the client's. And the web picker does compress before sending, via compressImage at maxWidth 2400 quality 0.85 - which matters, because AC5 says match the web and an AC that says match X inherits X's behaviour whether or not anyone checked it.  THREE THINGS THE CONTRACT CATCHES THAT A SWIFT AUTHOR WOULD OTHERWISE HIT.  First, the limit already exists TWICE - MAX_ATTACHMENTS_PER_MESSAGE on the edge, which rejects with a 400, and MAX_ATTACHMENTS in the web picker, which stops you selecting. A Swift constant is the third. If the client's limit ever exceeds the server's, the user waits through an upload and THEN gets the error, which is the worst ordering of those two failures. The guard compares all of them.  Second, the key is data_url in snake_case, not dataUrl. The edge reads item?.data_url and a camelCase key decodes to null, which surfaces as One attachment was not an image - a message that blames the bytes when the key was wrong. That is an hour of debugging for the second client implementation and it is now a pinned fact.
